o: Days inventory + days receivable − days payable
Days inventory + days payable − days receivable
CSH-001.e: CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO: the time cash is tied up in operations.
CSH-001.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice (Brealey–Myers–Allen, Principles of Corporate Finance; CFA Institute – Working capital management).
Analysis: CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO: the time from paying suppliers to collecting from customers – how long cash is 'locked' in operations. Stock sitting (DIO) and awaiting collection (DSO) lengthen it; supplier credit (DPO) shortens it.
Distractors: B swaps DSO and DPO signs; C is incomplete; D is working capital turnover.

CSH-002.q: Match each metric with its formula (365-day year):
p: Trade payables / cost of goods sold × 365
CSH-002.e: Average opening–closing balances can be used for more accuracy.
CSH-002.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Analysis: DSO = receivables / revenue × 365 (receivables arise from sales); DIO = inventory / COGS × 365 (inventory is at cost); DPO = trade payables / COGS × 365 (purchases relate to cost; purchases themselves are more precise).
Note: Average opening–closing balances reduce period-end distortion; seasonal businesses should use monthly averages.

CSH-003.q: A company has trade receivables of VND 30 billion and annual revenue of 365 billion. What is DSO (days)?
CSH-003.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Working: DSO = 30 / 365 × 365 = 30 days (average sales 1 billion a day; receivables equal 30 days of sales).
Note: Compare DSO with policy credit terms (e.g., net 30) – a much higher DSO signals weak collections.

CSH-004.q: Inventory is VND 40 billion and annual cost of goods sold is 292 billion. What is DIO (days)?
CSH-004.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Working: DIO = 40 / 292 × 365 = 40 × 1.25 = 50 days (average COGS 0.8 billion a day; 40 billion of stock covers 50 days).

CSH-005.q: Trade payables are VND 24 billion and annual COGS is 292 billion. What is DPO (days)?
CSH-005.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Working: DPO = 24 / 292 × 365 = 24 × 1.25 = 30 days (payables equal 30 days of COGS).

CSH-006.q: DIO = 50 days, DSO = 30 days, DPO = 30 days. What is the cash conversion cycle (days)?
CSH-006.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Working: CCC = DIO 50 + DSO 30 − DPO 30 = 50 days.
Note: Each CCC day ties up roughly a day of cost/sales; cutting CCC releases cash directly (CSH-007, CSH-067).

CSH-007.q: Annual revenue is VND 365 billion (1 billion per day on average). Reducing DSO by 10 days releases approximately how much cash from receivables (VND)?
CSH-007.e: 10 days × 1 billion per day = 10 billion = 10,000,000,000 VND.
CSH-007.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Working: Average sales = 365 / 365 = 1 billion a day. Cutting DSO by 10 days → receivables fall 10 × 1 = 10 billion = 10,000,000,000 VND released.
Note: That's a one-off cash benefit; the annual profit benefit = 10 billion × the interest rate saved.

CSH-008.e: Positive NWC means current assets are partly financed by long-term sources.
CSH-008.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Analysis: Net working capital = current assets − current liabilities. Positive NWC: some current assets funded long-term – safer liquidity; negative: short-term funds finance long-term assets – risky (except retailers with negative CCC – CSH-010).
Distractors: B is equity; C is net cash (negative = net debt); D is gross profit.

CSH-009.q: Select ALL measures that shorten the cash conversion cycle:
o: Shortening credit terms, offering early-payment discounts to customers
Negotiating longer supplier payment terms (without losing valuable discounts)
Doubling raw material reserves beyond needs
Loosening credit terms for all customers
CSH-009.e: Higher inventory and looser credit lengthen the CCC.
CSH-009.x:
Basis: Working capital management practice.
Analysis: To shorten CCC: (A) lower DSO – tighter credit, early-payment discounts; (B) lower DIO – optimise stock, clear slow movers; (C) raise DPO – negotiate longer terms (without losing valuable discounts – CSH-040).
Distractors: (D) doubling stock raises DIO; (E) looser credit raises DSO and bad-debt risk.

CSH-010.q: A negative cash conversion cycle means the business collects from customers before paying suppliers – suppliers are financing working capital.
CSH-010.e: True. Common in fast-turnover retail and e-commerce.
CSH-010.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Analysis: True. Negative CCC: DIO + DSO < DPO – cash sales (low DSO) and fast stock turns (low DIO) but delayed supplier payments → suppliers fund working capital. Common in retail chains, supermarkets, e-commerce.
Note: If sales fall, the advantage reverses – cash goes out to suppliers faster than it comes in.

CSH-011.q: A toy and gift retail chain must stock up heavily before the holiday season, so its working capital needs are clearly seasonal.
CSH-011.e: True. Short-term credit lines should match the seasonality.
CSH-011.x:
Basis: Working capital management practice.
Analysis: True. Toy and gift sales cluster around holidays → large pre-season stocking, spikes in inventory and payables/borrowing, then cash returns after the season. Working capital needs are seasonal → a revolving short-term credit line fits (matching principle – CSH-051).

CSH-012.q: Fast revenue growth can leave a business short of cash even while profitable, because cash is tied up in growing receivables and inventory.
CSH-012.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Analysis: True. Fast sales growth swells receivables and stock (e.g., with a 50-day CCC, an extra 100 billion of annual sales needs about 14 billion more working capital); if retained profit doesn't cover it, the firm runs short of cash while profitable – 'overtrading'. Growth needs a funding plan.

CSH-013.q: The metric that best reflects 'earnings quality' (whether profit turns into cash) is:
o: Net operating cash flow / profit after tax
CSH-013.e: A persistently low ratio (OCF far below profit) warrants investigation.
CSH-013.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice (earnings quality).
Analysis: OCF / net profit shows how much profit became cash. A steady ratio ≥ 1 (thanks to depreciation) is healthy; a persistently low one means profit is sitting in receivables or stock, or revenue is aggressive.
Distractors: B, C and D measure margins, growth and dividend policy – not cash conversion.

CSH-014.q: Persistently negative operating cash flow alongside positive accounting profit is a warning sign about earnings quality or working capital management.
CSH-014.e: True. Analyse changes in receivables, inventory and premature revenue recognition.
CSH-014.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice; VSA 240, VSA 570.
Analysis: True. Positive profit with persistently negative OCF means either bloated working capital (fast-rising receivables, stock) or low-quality earnings (early or fictitious revenue – ICR-127). Analyse receivables, stock, ageing and returns; for auditors it flags fraud and going-concern risk.

CSH-015.q: A business has profit after tax of VND 50 billion, depreciation 20 billion, receivables up 15 billion, inventory up 10 billion, payables up 5 billion (simplified). What is net operating cash flow under the indirect method (VND billion)?
CSH-015.x:
Basis: VAS 24 (indirect method – simplified); IAS 7.
Working: OCF = net profit 50 + depreciation 20 (non-cash) − receivables increase 15 − inventory increase 10 + payables increase 5 = 50 billion VND.
Note: Rising current assets consume cash; rising payables supply it. VAS 24 starts from profit before tax; IFRS 18 uses operating profit (IFR-024).

CSH-016.q: Match each liquidity ratio with its formula:
p: Cash and cash equivalents / current liabilities
CSH-016.e: Ratios measuring the ability to meet short-term obligations.
CSH-016.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice.
Analysis: Current = current assets / current liabilities; quick = (current assets − inventory) / current liabilities – excluding illiquid stock (CSH-021); cash = cash and equivalents / current liabilities – the strictest. From broad to narrow, they gauge short-term solvency.

CSH-017.q: Current assets are VND 120 billion, current liabilities 80 billion. What is the current ratio?
CSH-017.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice.
Working: Current ratio = 120 / 80 = 1.5 times.
Note: Reasonable levels vary by industry; look at the mix of current assets (CSH-022), not just the headline.

CSH-018.q: Current assets are VND 120 billion, of which inventory 40 billion; current liabilities 80 billion. What is the quick ratio?
CSH-018.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice.
Working: Quick ratio = (120 − 40) / 80 = 80 / 80 = 1.0 times.
Note: Some analysts also strip prepayments and doubtful receivables from the numerator for extra caution.

CSH-019.q: Cash and equivalents are VND 20 billion, current liabilities 80 billion. What is the cash ratio?
CSH-019.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice.
Working: Cash ratio = 20 / 80 = 0.25 times.
Note: A low ratio isn't necessarily bad with steady inflows and standby credit lines (CSH-057); pair it with OCF / current liabilities (CSH-023).

CSH-020.q: A very high current ratio (e.g., above 4) is always a good sign of financial management.
CSH-020.e: False. It may indicate capital tied up in idle cash, inventory or receivables, reducing efficiency.
CSH-020.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice.
Analysis: False. A very high current ratio (> 4) may signal idle capital: low-yielding cash, slow stock, doubtful receivables – dragging down ROE and ROIC. 'Good' liquidity balances safety with capital efficiency.

CSH-021.q: Inventory is excluded from the quick ratio numerator because it is the least liquid current asset and may lose value in a forced sale.
CSH-021.e: True. For perishable (food, pharmaceuticals) or fast-obsolescing goods (electronics, fashion), impairment risk is higher.
CSH-021.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice; VAS 02 (net realisable value).
Analysis: True. Inventory is usually the least liquid current asset: it must be sold before cash comes in, and fire sales go below cost. For perishables (food, pharma) or fast-obsolescing goods (electronics, fashion), impairment risk is higher → excluded from the quick ratio.

CSH-022.q: A business has a current ratio of 1.6 but a quick ratio of only 0.4. The most appropriate interpretation is:
o: Current assets are concentrated in inventory; liquidity depends on selling goods
The business has too much cash
The business has no current liabilities
CSH-022.e: A large gap between the two ratios indicates heavy inventory.
CSH-022.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice.
Analysis: Current 1.6 and quick 0.4 → inventory is (1.6 − 0.4) / 1.6 = 75% of current assets. Solvency depends on selling stock; check its quality (ageing, slow movers, allowances).
Distractors: B and D are wrong since large cash or receivables would raise the quick ratio; C – the ratio requires current liabilities.

CSH-023.q: Operating cash flow to current liabilities (OCF / current liabilities) reflects the ability to repay short-term debt from generated cash, complementing balance-based ratios.
CSH-023.e: True. Cash-flow ratios are less affected by reporting-date timing.
CSH-023.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice.
Analysis: True. OCF / current liabilities measures the ability to pay short-term debts from cash generated over the period, not a point-in-time balance (which can be 'window-dressed' by collecting or deferring payments). Combining balance-based and flow-based ratios gives a fuller liquidity picture.

CSH-024.q: A 13-week rolling cash forecast is mainly used to:
o: Manage weekly short-term liquidity and spot shortfalls early
CSH-024.e: 13-week forecasts usually use the direct method and are updated weekly.
CSH-024.x:
Basis: Treasury management practice; VAS 24.
Analysis: A 13-week (one-quarter) weekly rolling forecast (dropping the past week, adding a new one), built by the direct method – a short-term liquidity tool that flags cash-short weeks early to arrange funding or defer payments; vital in restructurings or distress.
Distractors: B uses long-range models; C and D aren't its purpose.

CSH-025.q: Short-term cash forecasts usually use the direct method (each receipt and payment), while long-term forecasts often use the indirect method from profit.
CSH-025.e: True. The direct method is detailed and suits weekly treasury control.
CSH-025.x:
Basis: Treasury management practice; VAS 24 (direct and indirect methods).
Analysis: True. Short-term: the direct method – each receipt (per customer collection schedules) and payment (payroll, suppliers, tax, interest) – precise on timing, suited to weekly treasury control. Long-term: the indirect method from forecast profit, adjusted for depreciation, working capital and capex – tied to the business plan.

CSH-026.q: Opening cash is VND 5 billion; expected receipts 30 billion, payments 33 billion; minimum cash policy 4 billion. How much must be borrowed this month (VND billion)?
CSH-026.e: Closing before borrowing = 5 + 30 − 33 = 2 billion; borrow 4 − 2 = 2 billion VND to reach the minimum.
CSH-026.x:
Basis: Treasury management practice (cash budget).
Working: Ending balance before borrowing = 5 + 30 − 33 = 2 billion. Shortfall to the minimum = 4 − 2 = 2 billion VND to borrow.
Note: If borrowing costs are material, include the interest in the next period's payments.

CSH-027.q: Arrange the steps for preparing a cash budget:
o: Determine surplus/deficit against the minimum cash balance
Plan borrowing or investment of surplus cash
CSH-027.e: The cash budget is a key output of the master budget.
CSH-027.x:
Basis: Treasury practice; master budgeting.
Analysis: Order: opening cash → forecast receipts (from the sales budget and credit policy) → forecast payments (purchases, payroll, expenses, tax, capex, debt service) → surplus/shortfall versus minimum cash → plan borrowing or investing surplus cash. The cash budget consolidates the outputs of the other budgets.

CSH-028.q: Select ALL common causes of cash forecast errors:
o: Overly optimistic assumptions about customer collection timing
Omitting large recurring payments (tax, SI, interest, capex)
Not updating raw material price and FX changes
Comparing forecasts with actuals weekly and analysing variances
CSH-028.e: Comparing actuals with forecasts is good practice to improve accuracy.
CSH-028.x:
Basis: Treasury management practice.
Analysis: Causes of forecast error: (A) optimistic collection assumptions – customers usually pay late; (B) missing large periodic outflows (quarterly tax, social insurance, interest, capex, Tet bonuses); (C) not updating input prices and FX.
Distractors: (D) Weekly forecast-versus-actual reviews are good practice that improve accuracy, not a cause of error.

CSH-029.q: Cash pooling lets a group use surplus balances of one unit to cover deficits of another, reducing interest costs.
CSH-029.e: True. Consider related-party, foreign exchange and tax rules when applying it.
CSH-029.x:
Basis: Group treasury practice; Decree 132/2020/ND-CP (related-party transactions).
Analysis: True. Cash pooling combines entity balances (physically or notionally) to offset surpluses and deficits, cutting external borrowing and interest. Legal points: intra-group loans are related-party transactions (arm's-length rates, the 30% of EBITDA interest cap), FX rules for cross-border flows, and foreign contractor tax on interest paid abroad.

CSH-030.q: A payment calendar with fixed dates for payroll, SI, taxes and interest helps a business arrange funds proactively.
CSH-030.e: True. For example, monthly SI is due by the end of the following month; monthly VAT returns by the 20th.
CSH-030.x:
Basis: Treasury practice; Tax Administration Law 38/2019/QH14 (monthly filing deadlines); Social Insurance Law 41/2024/QH15.
Analysis: True. A payment calendar of fixed outflows (payroll, social insurance, tax, debt service, rent) lets funds be lined up in advance, avoiding late payment (0.03% a day on tax). E.g., monthly VAT by the 20th of the next month; social insurance by the last day of the following month (per the question's source).

CSH-031.q: Short-term investment of surplus cash should prioritise in the order:
CSH-031.e: Liquidity reserves should not be invested in risky or illiquid assets.
CSH-031.x:
Basis: Treasury practice (surplus cash investment policy).
Analysis: Priority: safety (no loss of principal) → liquidity (available when needed) → yield. Liquidity buffers belong in short-term deposits at sound banks or CDs, not in risky, illiquid shares or corporate bonds.
Distractors: B, C and D put yield first – risking illiquidity exactly when cash is needed.

CSH-032.q: Two-level payment approval (maker–checker) on e-banking with tiered limits is a key treasury control.
CSH-032.e: True. Combine with daily bank reconciliation and control over beneficiary changes.
CSH-032.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (segregation, authorisation); treasury practice.
Analysis: True. Maker–checker: one person enters, another approves; tiered limits (large payments need seniors or dual approval) – stopping any individual from moving money alone. Pair with daily bank reconciliation and controls over payee changes (ICR-085) against fraud and BEC.

CSH-033.q: Cash Flow at Risk analysis estimates the maximum shortfall in cash flow at a given confidence level due to market movements (prices, FX, interest rates).
CSH-033.e: True. Suitable for businesses with imported inputs (cotton, yarn, electronic components, plastic resin).
CSH-033.x:
Basis: Financial risk management practice (Cash Flow at Risk – extending VaR).
Analysis: True. CFaR estimates the maximum cash-flow shortfall over a period at a confidence level (e.g., 95%) from moves in input prices, FX and rates – often via Monte Carlo on a cash-flow model. It helps importers of cotton, yarn, components or plastic resin size hedges and standby credit.

CSH-034.q: Cash forecasts should be built with several scenarios (base, optimistic, pessimistic) to prepare liquidity contingency plans.
CSH-034.e: True. The pessimistic case should be linked to standby credit lines.
CSH-034.x:
Basis: Treasury practice; COSO ERM 2017 (scenario analysis).
Analysis: True. Single-point forecasts hide risk; base, upside and downside scenarios show the range of possible shortfalls. The downside case needs concrete actions: standby credit lines, cost cuts, deferred capex, collections drives.

CSH-035.q: Which metric do banks commonly use to assess the repayment capacity of a project/borrower?
o: Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) = cash available for debt service / principal and interest due
CSH-035.e: A DSCR below 1 means cash flow cannot cover debt due.
CSH-035.x:
Basis: Bank lending and project finance practice.
Analysis: DSCR = cash available for debt service (often EBITDA − tax − maintenance capex, or CFADS) / principal and interest due. DSCR < 1: cash doesn't cover debt service; banks typically require at least 1.2–1.3x.
Distractors: B, C and D measure margins, asset efficiency and dividend policy.

CSH-036.q: Cash available for debt service next year is VND 15 billion; total principal and interest due is 10 billion. What is the DSCR?
CSH-036.x:
Basis: Bank lending practice.
Working: DSCR = 15 / 10 = 1.5 times – cash exceeds debt service by 50%.
Note: Compare with the covenant (e.g., 1.2 minimum) to gauge headroom before breach (CSH-037).

CSH-037.q: Breaching loan covenants, such as minimum DSCR or maximum debt/EBITDA, may lead the bank to demand early repayment.
CSH-037.e: True. Finance should monitor covenants quarterly.
CSH-037.x:
Basis: Credit agreement practice; VAS 21/IAS 1 (classifying debt after covenant breaches).
Analysis: True. Breaching covenants (minimum DSCR, maximum debt/EBITDA, liquidity ratios) is usually an event of default allowing the bank to accelerate repayment, raise rates or stop drawdowns. Accounting effect: long-term loans may become current; for auditors it's a going-concern indicator (VSA-084). Finance should track covenants quarterly and forecast ahead.

o: A 2% discount if paid within 10 days; otherwise pay in full within 30 days
A 10% discount if paid within 2 days
CSH-038.e: A common term in domestic and international trade.
CSH-038.x:
Basis: Trade and working capital practice.
Analysis: '2/10, net 30': a 2% discount if paid within 10 days; otherwise the full amount within 30. The buyer effectively 'pays' 2% to keep cash 20 more days – a very high implicit cost (CSH-039).
Distractors: B, C and D misread the notation.

CSH-039.q: Under '2/10, net 30', what is the opportunity cost (implied simple annual rate, 365 days) of NOT taking the discount (%, rounded to 1 decimal)?
CSH-039.e: 2/98 × 365/20 = 37.2% per year — usually far above bank rates, so borrowing to take the discount pays.
CSH-039.x:
Basis: Working capital practice.
Working: Cost of forgoing the discount = 2 / (100 − 2) × 365 / (30 − 10) = 0.020408 × 18.25 = 0.3724 → 37.2% a year (simple). Compounded: (1 + 2/98)^(365/20) − 1 ≈ 44.6%.
Note: The denominator is 98 because the buyer effectively 'borrows' 98 (the discounted amount) for 20 days.

CSH-040.q: If a business can borrow at 9% per year, borrowing to pay early and take a '2/10, net 30' discount is beneficial.
CSH-040.e: True. The cost of forgoing the discount (~37%/year) exceeds 9% interest.
CSH-040.x:
Basis: Working capital practice.
Analysis: True. Forgoing the discount costs about 37% a year (CSH-039), far above 9% bank interest → borrowing to pay early saves roughly 28 percentage points a year on that amount.
Note: Provided credit headroom exists and covenants aren't breached.

CSH-041.q: Select ALL effective receivables management tools:
o: Credit scoring and approving limits per customer
Ageing reports and staged collection reminders
Continuing deliveries to overdue customers without review
CSH-041.e: Supplying overdue customers further raises loss risk.
CSH-041.x:
Basis: Working capital practice; COSO 2013 (order-to-cash).
Analysis: Effective tools: (A) credit scoring and customer limits; (B) ageing reports and staged dunning (e.g., at 7, 15, 30 days overdue); (C) early-payment discounts; (D) factoring and document discounting – turning receivables into cash.
Distractors: (E) Shipping to overdue customers without review raises loss risk – an automatic credit hold is needed.

CSH-042.q: The economic order quantity (EOQ) model minimises:
CSH-042.e: EOQ = √(2DS/H); D: annual demand; S: cost per order; H: holding cost per unit per year.
CSH-042.x:
Basis: EOQ model (Harris, 1913) – inventory management practice.
Analysis: EOQ minimises total ordering cost (D/Q × S – falls with larger lots) plus holding cost (Q/2 × H – rises with larger lots); the optimum is where they're equal: EOQ = √(2DS/H).
Distractors: B – purchase price doesn't vary with lot size in the basic model; C and D aren't the objective.
Note: It assumes even demand and no quantity discounts – adjust when reality differs.

CSH-043.q: Demand for plastic resin is 40,000 bags/year; ordering cost VND 500,000 per order; holding cost VND 10,000 per bag per year. What is the EOQ (bags)?
CSH-043.x:
Basis: EOQ model.
Working: EOQ = √(2 × 40,000 × 500,000 / 10,000) = √(40,000,000,000 / 10,000) = √4,000,000 = 2,000 bags.
Check: orders = 40,000 / 2,000 = 20 → ordering cost 20 × 0.5 = 10 million; holding 2,000/2 × 10,000 = 10 million – equal at the optimum.

CSH-044.q: A plant uses an average of 500 kg of steel sheet per day; lead time 7 days; safety stock 1,000 kg. What is the reorder point (kg)?
CSH-044.x:
Basis: Inventory management practice (reorder point – ROP).
Working: ROP = daily usage × lead time + safety stock = 500 × 7 + 1,000 = 3,500 + 1,000 = 4,500 kg.
Note: Safety stock buffers demand and lead-time variability; more of it means fewer stockouts but higher holding costs.

CSH-045.q: Match each ABC inventory class with its control approach:
p: Class A – few items, high value
Tight control, frequent counts, detailed forecasting
Class C – many items, low value
CSH-045.e: ABC (Pareto) analysis allocates inventory control effort.
CSH-045.x:
Basis: ABC analysis (Pareto principle) in inventory management.
Analysis: Group A – about 10–20% of SKUs holding 70–80% of value: tight control, frequent cycle counts, detailed forecasts; Group B – moderate: periodic control; Group C – many low-value SKUs: simple control, large infrequent orders.
Note: Combine with XYZ analysis (demand stability) to choose replenishment policies.

CSH-046.q: For short-shelf-life goods (food, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics), FEFO (first-expired, first-out) is more suitable than FIFO to reduce expired goods.
CSH-046.e: True. FEFO prioritises lots closest to expiry.
CSH-046.x:
Basis: Warehouse practice (Good Distribution Practice for pharmaceuticals).
Analysis: True. FEFO (First Expired, First Out) ships the earliest-expiring lot first, even if received later – reducing write-offs and allowances. For food, pharma and cosmetics, expiry matters more than receipt date; manage by lot/expiry in the system.
Note: FEFO governs physical picking; the accounting cost flow (FIFO, average) still follows VAS 02.

CSH-047.q: The Miller–Orr cash model sets upper and lower limits and a return point; at the upper limit invest surplus cash, at the lower limit replenish cash.
CSH-047.e: True. Suitable when cash flows fluctuate randomly.
CSH-047.x:
Basis: Miller–Orr model (1966) of cash management.
Analysis: True. It sets a lower limit (L – minimum cash), a return point Z = L + ∛(3Fσ²/4i) and an upper limit H = 3Z − 2L. Hitting H → invest (H − Z) back to Z; hitting L → sell investments or borrow (Z − L) up to Z. It suits random, hard-to-forecast cash flows, unlike Baumol (steady flows).

CSH-048.q: Stretching supplier payments excessively (beyond agreed terms) may damage reputation, forfeit discounts and risk supply disruption.
CSH-048.e: True. Payables management must balance liquidity and supplier relationships.
CSH-048.x:
Basis: Working capital and supply chain practice.
Analysis: True. Paying beyond terms lifts DPO briefly but damages credibility, forfeits discounts (high hidden cost – CSH-039), and invites price rises, tighter credit, lower priority or supply stoppages – disruption risk. Payables management balances liquidity with supplier relationships; supply chain finance is a healthier fix (CSH-064).

CSH-049.q: Non-recourse factoring transfers customers' credit risk to the factor.
CSH-049.e: True. With recourse factoring, the business still bears the risk if customers do not pay.
CSH-049.x:
Basis: Trade finance practice; IFRS 9 (derecognition – IFR-102).
Analysis: True. Non-recourse factoring: the factor bears customer insolvency risk → credit risk transfers and the receivable may be derecognised. With recourse: the seller repays if the customer defaults → risk stays, in substance a secured loan (IFR-102). Non-recourse fees are correspondingly higher.

CSH-050.q: An inventory turnover of 7.3 times per year corresponds to average days in inventory of about:
CSH-050.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice.
Working: Days in inventory = 365 / turnover = 365 / 7.3 = 50 days.
Distractors: 73, 30 and 7 days are miscalculated.

CSH-051.q: The matching principle in financing requires:
o: Long-term assets financed by long-term sources; seasonal working capital by short-term sources
All assets financed by short-term loans
Current assets financed by long-term loans
CSH-051.e: Using short-term loans to build factories or buy machinery creates major liquidity risk.
CSH-051.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice (maturity matching principle).
Analysis: Long-term assets (plant, machinery) and permanent working capital are funded long-term (equity, term loans); temporary, seasonal working capital is funded short-term. Funding maturity matches the period over which assets generate cash to repay.
Distractors: B and D mismatch maturities – refinancing risk; C is safe but costly, not optimal.

CSH-052.q: Using short-term loans to build a new factory violates the matching principle and increases liquidity risk.
CSH-052.e: True. Long-term projects need medium/long-term funding matching their payback.
CSH-052.x:
Basis: Matching principle; bank lending practice.
Analysis: True. A new plant pays back over years, but short-term loans must be repaid or rolled within 12 months → if the bank won't roll or rates rise, the firm must find repayment while the project generates no cash – severe liquidity risk. Medium- or long-term loans with suitable grace periods are needed.

CSH-053.q: Match each hedging instrument with the situation of an electronic components importer paying USD in 3 months:
p: Buy USD in advance at a fixed rate for the payment date
Right to buy USD at an agreed rate, paying a premium
Convert a floating-rate loan to fixed
CSH-053.e: Businesses should have a board-approved hedging policy.
CSH-053.x:
Basis: Financial risk management practice; IFRS 9 (hedge accounting – IFR-098).
Analysis: Forward – fix the USD rate for the payment date (removes risk but forgoes gains if USD falls); call option – the right to buy USD at a set rate for a premium (protects against a rise, keeps upside if USD falls); interest rate swap – convert floating-rate debt to fixed.
Note: The hedging policy should be board-approved and forbid speculation.

CSH-054.q: A letter of credit (L/C) reduces exporters' non-payment risk because the issuing bank undertakes to pay against complying documents.
CSH-054.e: True. L/Cs are a safe international payment method for sellers.
CSH-054.x:
Basis: UCP 600 (ICC) – Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits.
Analysis: True. Under an L/C, the issuing bank independently undertakes to pay on presentation of documents complying with its terms – shifting risk from the buyer's credit to the bank's (plus documentary risk). A confirmed L/C also protects against issuing-bank and country risk.
Note: Banks deal in documents, not goods – minor discrepancies can lead to refusal.

CSH-055.q: Select ALL main financial risks a manufacturer importing raw materials must manage:
o: Commodity price risk (cotton, steel, plastic resin)
Share price movements of other companies the company does not hold
CSH-055.e: The first five are material financial risks; shares not held do not affect the company.
CSH-055.x:
Basis: Financial risk management practice; IFRS 7 (financial risk disclosures).
Analysis: Key financial risks: (A) FX – foreign-currency inputs and debt; (B) interest rate – floating debt; (C) liquidity – heavy working capital; (D) credit – distributor receivables; (E) commodity price – cotton, steel, resin swings.
Distractors: (F) Other companies' share prices don't matter if none are held.

CSH-056.q: When most revenue is in VND but raw material costs and debt are in USD, the business faces FX risk when the VND depreciates.
CSH-056.e: True. Natural hedges (VND borrowing, localising inputs) or derivatives can be used.
CSH-056.x:
Basis: FX risk management practice.
Analysis: True. VND revenue with USD costs and debt → when VND weakens, VND-denominated costs and obligations rise while revenue doesn't → margins and cash flow shrink, plus revaluation losses. Natural hedges: borrow in VND, localise inputs, index prices to FX; or use forwards and options (CSH-053).

CSH-057.q: An unused credit line serves as:
o: Standby liquidity for unexpected cash shortfalls
A way to increase accounting profit
CSH-057.e: Businesses often pay commitment fees on unused lines.
CSH-057.x:
Basis: Treasury and bank lending practice.
Analysis: Undrawn credit lines are a liquidity reserve – drawn when cash falls short unexpectedly (late customers, input price spikes). Commitment fees are usually paid on the undrawn portion; banks may cancel lines on covenant breaches.
Distractors: B – no accounting profit; C – debt doesn't replace charter capital; D is unrelated to tax.

CSH-058.q: A bank payment guarantee lets a business buy on credit from large suppliers without depositing the full amount in cash.
CSH-058.e: True. Guarantee fees and collateral are set by the bank.
CSH-058.x:
Basis: Trade finance practice; State Bank rules on bank guarantees.
Analysis: True. With a payment guarantee the bank pays if the business doesn't → large suppliers sell on credit without full cash deposits, preserving operating cash. Costs: guarantee fees, partial margin deposits and collateral as the bank requires.

CSH-059.q: A business borrows VND 10 billion at 9% per year; the bank requires a non-interest-bearing compensating balance of 10% of the loan. What is the effective interest rate (%)?
CSH-059.e: Interest 0.9 billion / usable funds 9 billion = 10% per year.
CSH-059.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice (effective rate with compensating balances).
Working: Interest = 10 × 9% = 0.9 billion. Usable funds = 10 − 10% × 10 = 9 billion. Effective rate = 0.9 / 9 = 10% a year.
Note: Generally: nominal rate / (1 − compensating balance ratio) = 9% / 0.9 = 10%.

CSH-060.q: Credit concentration risk arises when most credit sales come from a few distributors; customer limits and suitable collateral are needed.
CSH-060.e: True. Monitor revenue and receivable shares of top customers.
CSH-060.x:
Basis: Trade credit risk practice; COSO ERM 2017 (concentration risk).
Analysis: True. With most credit sales to a few distributors, one default can cause big losses and cash shortfalls. Controls: customer limits, security (bank guarantees, deposits), credit insurance; track top-customer revenue and receivable shares (KRIs – ICR-160).

CSH-061.q: Annual revenue is VND 600 billion; average trade receivables 50 billion. What is receivables turnover (times per year)?
CSH-061.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice.
Working: Receivables turnover = 600 / 50 = 12 times a year → DSO = 365 / 12 ≈ 30.4 days.

CSH-062.q: A plant uses 2 tonnes of its main raw material per day and holds 60 tonnes. How many days of usage does the stock cover?
CSH-062.x:
Basis: Inventory management practice (days of cover).
Working: 60 / 2 = 30 days.
Note: Compare with lead time and safety stock (CSH-044) to time the next order.

CSH-063.q: Collecting customer advances (dealer deposits) improves cash flow and reduces working capital needs.
CSH-063.e: True. It is interest-free funding from customers.
CSH-063.x:
Basis: Working capital practice; VAS 14/IFRS 15 (advances are liabilities).
Analysis: True. Dealer deposits and advances arrive before delivery → earlier cash, lower working capital needs (akin to higher DPO), and interest-free funding. They're recorded as liabilities (customer advances – ACC-099), not revenue.

CSH-064.q: Supply chain finance (reverse factoring) is where:
o: A bank pays suppliers early based on the buyer's credit; the buyer pays the bank at maturity
The business sells its receivables to a bank
The supplier lends to the buyer
CSH-064.e: Suppliers get paid early at low cost; the buyer keeps its payment terms.
CSH-064.x:
Basis: Supply chain finance practice.
Analysis: Reverse factoring is buyer-led (usually a strong credit): the bank pays suppliers early on the buyer's invoice approval, priced on the buyer's credit (cheaper than the supplier's borrowing); the buyer pays the bank at maturity – keeping or extending DPO.
Distractors: B is ordinary factoring; C is inventory-secured lending; D is supplier credit.

CSH-065.q: A business sells VND 1 billion of receivables to a factor at a fee of 2% of the receivables (ignoring interest). What is the factoring cost (VND)?
CSH-065.x:
Basis: Trade finance practice.
Working: Factoring fee = 1,000,000,000 × 2% = 20,000,000 VND.
Note: Compare with borrowing: if cash arrives 60 days early, 2% is about 12% a year (2% × 365/60) – dearer than a bank loan, so weigh it.

CSH-066.q: Cash forecasting practice is often tiered: daily for 1–2 weeks, weekly for 13 weeks, monthly for the next 12 months.
CSH-066.e: True. Each tier serves a different management purpose.
CSH-066.x:
Basis: Treasury management practice.
Analysis: True. Layered forecasting: daily for 1–2 weeks – balances and daily payments; weekly for 13 weeks – liquidity and short-term borrowing (CSH-024); monthly for 12 months – budgets, funding plans, covenants. Each layer has its own granularity and purpose.

CSH-067.q: Average cost of goods sold is VND 0.8 billion per day. Reducing days in inventory by 5 releases how much cash (VND billion)?
CSH-067.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Working: Cash released = 5 days × 0.8 billion a day = 4 billion VND (inventory falls by 5 days of COGS).

CSH-068.q: Overstocking short-shelf-life finished goods (food, pharmaceuticals) raises expiry risk, requiring provisions or destruction and causing cash loss.
CSH-068.e: True. Balance customer service levels against inventory costs.
CSH-068.x:
Basis: Inventory management practice; VAS 02, Circular 48/2019/TT-BTC (write-downs).
Analysis: True. Overstocking short-life finished goods → near-expiry or expired stock must be discounted, written down (ACC-090) or destroyed – cash spent on buying or making it is lost. Balance service levels (avoiding stockouts) with holding costs; use FEFO (CSH-046) and channel-level demand forecasts.

CSH-069.q: The most suitable financing for working capital that rises with the maize silage harvest season is:
CSH-069.e: Temporary needs should be funded by flexible short-term sources.
CSH-069.x:
Basis: Matching principle (CSH-051).
Analysis: Funding needs peaking with the biomass corn harvest are temporary and recurring – suited to a revolving short-term line: draw during procurement, repay as feed sales are collected, paying interest only on amounts drawn.
Distractors: B and C – long-term funds for a temporary need leave idle, costly capital off-season; D cuts production capacity.

CSH-070.q: Trade receivables VND 30 billion, inventory 40 billion, trade payables 24 billion. What is the net operating working capital requirement (receivables + inventory − payables) (VND billion)?
CSH-070.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Working: Operating net working capital = receivables 30 + inventory 40 − payables 24 = 46 billion VND.
Note: Check via days (CSH-003–006): DSO 30 × sales 1 billion/day = 30; DIO 50 × COGS 0.8 billion/day = 40; DPO 30 × 0.8 = 24 → 30 + 40 − 24 = 46.

CSH-071.q: An expanding business may have positive operating cash flow but negative free cash flow due to heavy investment; this is not bad if projects have positive NPV and suitable financing.
CSH-071.e: True. Assess according to the growth stage.
CSH-071.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice (business life cycle, NPV).
Analysis: True. FCF = OCF − capex; an expanding firm spends heavily, so FCF may be negative despite positive OCF. That's fine if projects have positive NPV and matched funding (CSH-051). It's worrying when negative FCF persists because OCF is weak, or capex is scattered and short-term-funded.

CSH-072.q: Average fixed weekly payments (payroll, rent, interest…) are VND 3 billion. With a policy of a minimum cash balance equal to 2 weeks of fixed payments, what is the minimum balance (VND billion)?
CSH-072.x:
Basis: Treasury practice (minimum cash policy).
Working: Minimum cash = 3 × 2 = 6 billion VND.
Note: The buffer depends on inflow volatility and standby credit (CSH-057); firms with large undrawn lines can hold less cash.

CSH-073.q: Keeping all deposits at one bank raises counterparty risk; businesses should spread deposits with limits per bank.
CSH-073.e: True. Treasury policy should set limits by bank rating.
CSH-073.x:
Basis: Treasury practice (counterparty risk).
Analysis: True. With all deposits at one bank, a bank problem (special control, system outage) leaves the firm unable to pay; deposit insurance covers individuals only, with low limits. Treasury policy should cap deposits per bank by credit rating and maximum share.

CSH-074.q: Shortening payment terms for small suppliers (household producers, subcontract workshops) stabilises their cash flow and loyalty but raises the company's working capital needs; this must be balanced in purchasing policy.
CSH-074.e: True. It is a trade-off between supply security and cost of capital.
CSH-074.x:
Basis: Working capital and supply chain practice.
Analysis: True. Paying thinly capitalised small suppliers quickly steadies their cash, quality and loyalty – supply security; but DPO falls and the company's working capital and capital costs rise. Balance by segmenting suppliers, or use supply chain finance (CSH-064) so suppliers get paid early while the company keeps its terms.

CSH-075.q: Under the indirect method, which item REDUCES net operating cash flow relative to profit?
CSH-075.e: Rising receivables mean revenue not yet collected in cash.
CSH-075.x:
Basis: VAS 24 (indirect method).
Analysis: Rising receivables: revenue is in profit but not yet collected → deducted from profit in OCF.
Distractors: B – depreciation is non-cash and added back; C – rising payables mean expenses not yet paid → added; D – falling inventory frees cash → added.

CSH-076.q: Annual revenue is VND 730 billion; trade receivables are 60 billion. What is DSO (365-day year)?
CSH-076.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Working: DSO = 60 / 730 × 365 = 60 / 2 = 30 days (sales of 2 billion a day).

CSH-077.q: Annual COGS is VND 547.5 billion; inventory is 45 billion. What is DIO?
CSH-077.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Working: Average COGS = 547.5 / 365 = 1.5 billion a day. DIO = 45 / 1.5 = 30 days.

CSH-078.q: DIO = 45 days, DSO = 35 days, DPO = 60 days. What is the cash conversion cycle?
CSH-078.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Working: CCC = DIO 45 + DSO 35 − DPO 60 = 20 days.
Note: A long DPO shortens CCC; check whether 60 days is per terms or late payment (CSH-048).

CSH-079.q: The operating cycle equals days inventory plus days receivable, before deducting days payable.
CSH-079.e: True. Operating cycle = DIO + DSO; deducting DPO gives the cash conversion cycle.
CSH-079.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Analysis: True. Operating cycle = DIO + DSO: from receiving stock to collecting sales cash. Subtracting DPO (supplier credit) gives the CCC – the part of the cycle the firm funds itself.

CSH-080.q: DIO = 40 days, DSO = 25 days, DPO = 35 days. What is the operating cycle?
CSH-080.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Working: Operating cycle = 40 + 25 = 65 days; CCC = 65 − 35 = 30 days.

CSH-081.q: Which decision INCREASES working capital requirements?
CSH-081.e: Longer credit increases receivables and ties up cash longer; the other options reduce working capital needs.
o: Extending customer credit terms from 30 to 60 days
Reducing safety stock thanks to better forecasting
CSH-081.x:
Basis: Working capital practice.
Analysis: Extending customer credit from 30 to 60 days → higher DSO and receivables → cash locked longer → higher working capital needs.
Distractors: B – raises DPO; C – lowers DIO; D – advances arrive early (CSH-063) – all three reduce needs.

CSH-082.q: Current assets are VND 150 billion and current liabilities 100 billion. The company uses 20 billion of cash to pay suppliers. What is the current ratio after the transaction?
CSH-082.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice.
Working: Before: 150 / 100 = 1.5. After paying suppliers 20 billion in cash: (150 − 20) / (100 − 20) = 130 / 80 = 1.625 times.
Note: Real liquidity didn't improve (cash fell) but the ratio rose – see CSH-083.

CSH-083.q: When the current ratio exceeds 1, using cash to repay current liabilities increases the ratio.
CSH-083.e: True. Numerator and denominator fall by the same amount; with a ratio above 1 the result rises. It is also a period-end 'window dressing' technique analysts should watch for.
CSH-083.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice.
Analysis: True. For a/b > 1, subtracting the same x from both: (a − x)/(b − x) > a/b. Firms may pay down current liabilities just before year-end to 'window-dress' the current ratio. Analysts should use average balances, check early next-period movements and add cash-flow ratios (CSH-023).
Note: Conversely, when the ratio is below 1 this lowers it.

CSH-084.e: DIR = (Cash + short-term investments + receivables) / average daily cash operating expenses.
o: The number of days the business can pay operating expenses from highly liquid assets without additional revenue
Times interest is covered by EBIT
CSH-084.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice (Defensive Interval Ratio).
Analysis: DIR = (cash + short-term investments + receivables) / average daily cash operating expenses – how many days liquid assets alone can fund operations without new revenue. Useful for stress-testing sudden revenue loss.
Distractors: B is DIO; C is payback; D is interest cover (CSH-123).

CSH-085.q: Cash, short-term investments and receivables total VND 36 billion; average daily cash operating expenses are 1.2 billion. What is the defensive interval?
CSH-085.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice.
Working: DIR = 36 / 1.2 = 30 days.
Note: Cash operating expenses exclude depreciation and provisions (non-cash).

CSH-086.q: Under VAS 24, select ALL items that are cash equivalents:
CSH-086.e: Cash equivalents: short-term investments maturing within 3 months of acquisition, readily convertible to known amounts of cash and subject to insignificant risk of value change. Shares fluctuate in price and are not cash equivalents.
o: Term deposits with original maturity of no more than 3 months
Treasury bills maturing within 3 months of purchase
CSH-086.x:
Basis: VAS 24 – Cash flow statement.
Analysis: Cash equivalents are short-term investments maturing within 3 months of purchase, readily convertible to known amounts of cash and subject to insignificant value risk: (A) deposits with original terms ≤ 3 months; (B) treasury bills maturing within 3 months of purchase.
Distractors: (C) shares fluctuate, with no known cash amount; (D) a 6-month original term exceeds 3 months (CSH-087).

CSH-087.q: A bank deposit with a 6-month original maturity is presented as a cash equivalent on the statement of financial position.
CSH-087.e: False. Original maturity over 3 months does not qualify; it is presented as a held-to-maturity investment.
CSH-087.x:
Basis: VAS 24; Circular 99/2025/TT-BTC (held-to-maturity investments line).
Analysis: False. The test is the original term (from placement), not time remaining; a 6-month original term > 3 months → not a cash equivalent; it's shown as a held-to-maturity (short-term) investment. Placing such deposits is an investing cash flow.

CSH-088.e: FCF = OCF − Capex: cash left after maintaining/expanding capacity, available for debt service, dividends or accumulation.
o: Net operating cash flow − capital expenditure
CSH-088.x:
Basis: Corporate finance and valuation practice (Damodaran; CFA Institute).
Analysis: FCF (simple) = OCF − capex: cash left after maintaining and expanding capacity, available for debt service, dividends or saving. Valuation also uses FCFF (before interest) and FCFE (after debt flows).
Distractors: B, C and D aren't free cash flow.

CSH-089.q: Net operating cash flow is VND 80 billion; fixed-asset purchases are 50 billion. What is free cash flow?
CSH-089.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Working: FCF = 80 − 50 = 30 billion VND.
Note: Separate maintenance from growth capex to judge sustainable FCF.

CSH-090.q: Match each cash flow with its activity on the cash flow statement (non-financial company):
CSH-090.e: VAS 24 classifies cash flows into operating, investing and financing activities.
p: Cash paid to suppliers of goods
Cash paid to purchase fixed assets
CSH-090.x:
Basis: VAS 24.
Analysis: Payments to suppliers → operating (tied to principal revenue); fixed-asset purchases → investing (long-term assets); loan proceeds → financing (changes in capital size and structure) – ACC-035, ACC-036.

CSH-091.q: Dividends and profits paid to owners are presented in cash flows from financing activities.
CSH-091.e: True. Under VAS 24 and form B03-DN, dividends paid are financing activities.
CSH-091.x:
Basis: VAS 24; form B03-DN under Circular 99/2025/TT-BTC.
Analysis: True. Dividends and profits paid to owners are financing (owner transactions). Note: dividends and interest received are investing (non-financial entities); under IFRS 18, interest paid is also financing (IFR-025).

CSH-092.q: Under the Baumol model, the optimal cash conversion amount (C*) equals (T: annual cash need; F: cost per conversion; i: investment rate):
CSH-092.e: C* = √(2TF/i), balancing transaction costs and the opportunity cost of holding cash – similar to EOQ.
CSH-092.x:
Basis: Baumol model (1952) of cash management.
Analysis: C* = √(2TF / i): balancing transaction costs (T/C × F – falling with larger C) and the opportunity cost of holding cash (C/2 × i – rising with larger C); it mirrors EOQ (CSH-042) with T ↔ D, F ↔ S, i ↔ H.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong formulas.

CSH-093.q: Annual cash need T = VND 3,600 million; cost per securities sale F = 2 million; investment rate i = 9% per year. What is the Baumol optimal cash amount?
CSH-093.x:
Basis: Baumol model.
Working: C* = √(2 × 3,600 × 2 / 0.09) = √(14,400 / 0.09) = √160,000 = 400 million VND.
Check: transfers = 3,600 / 400 = 9 → transaction cost 9 × 2 = 18 million; opportunity cost 400/2 × 9% = 18 million – equal at the optimum.

CSH-094.q: The Baumol model assumes steady, predictable cash outflows; when cash flows fluctuate randomly the Miller–Orr model is more suitable.
CSH-094.e: True. Miller–Orr uses upper and lower limits and a return point for random cash flows.
CSH-094.x:
Basis: Baumol model; Miller–Orr model.
Analysis: True. Baumol assumes steady, known outflows (like EOQ) – suited to stable spending. Real cash flows are often random → Miller–Orr uses upper and lower limits with a return point, its spread widening with cash-flow variance (CSH-047, CSH-095).

CSH-095.q: Under Miller–Orr: lower limit VND 2 billion, spread 6 billion. What is the return point?
CSH-095.e: Return point = lower limit + spread/3 = 2 + 2 = 4 billion; upper limit = 2 + 6 = 8 billion.
CSH-095.x:
Basis: Miller–Orr model.
Working: Return point Z = L + spread/3 = 2 + 6/3 = 4 billion VND; upper limit H = L + spread = 2 + 6 = 8 billion VND.
Note: Spread = 3 × ∛(3Fσ²/4i); Z sits a third of the way up (not the middle) because holding cash has an opportunity cost, making lower balances optimal.

CSH-096.q: Under Miller–Orr, when the cash balance hits the upper limit, the business:
CSH-096.e: It brings the balance back to the return point; at the lower limit it sells securities equal to (return point − lower limit).
o: Buys short-term securities equal to (upper limit − return point)
CSH-096.x:
Basis: Miller–Orr model.
Analysis: At the upper limit H → buy short-term securities of (H − Z) to return to Z. At the lower limit L → sell securities (or borrow) of (Z − L).
Distractors: B and C apply at the lower limit; D wastes yield on surplus cash.

CSH-097.q: Revenue is VND 365 billion per year (all on credit). Credit terms are extended from 30 to 45 days with unchanged revenue; cost of capital 10% per year. What is the additional annual financing cost of higher receivables?
CSH-097.e: Receivables rise by 15 days × 1 billion/day = 15 billion; cost = 15 × 10% = 1.5 billion per year.
CSH-097.x:
Basis: Trade credit practice (credit policy analysis).
Working: Sales average 1 billion a day. Receivables rise = (45 − 30) × 1 = 15 billion. Extra capital cost = 15 × 10% = 1.5 billion VND a year.
Note: More precisely, capital tied up is measured at the cost (variable cost) of receivables, not the selling price.

CSH-098.q: Loosening credit policy is worthwhile only when incremental contribution margin exceeds the combined financing cost of extra receivables, bad debts and extra collection costs.
CSH-098.e: True. This is the marginal cost–benefit analysis of credit policy.
CSH-098.x:
Basis: Trade credit practice (marginal analysis).
Analysis: True. Looser credit pays when the contribution margin on extra sales > the capital cost of extra receivables (CSH-097) + extra bad debts (CSH-099) + extra admin and collection costs. Use contribution (not revenue) since only that is real benefit.

CSH-099.q: A new credit policy adds VND 20 billion of revenue; expected bad debts are 3% of the extra revenue. What is the expected bad-debt loss?
CSH-099.x:
Basis: Trade credit practice.
Working: Expected bad debts = 20 × 3% = 0.6 billion VND.
Note: Combined with CSH-097 and CSH-098: at a 25% contribution margin, extra profit = 20 × 25% = 5 billion > 1.5 + 0.6 = 2.1 billion → the policy pays (before collection costs).

CSH-100.q: Which factor is NOT part of the 5C credit assessment model?
CSH-100.e: The 5Cs are Character, Capacity, Capital, Collateral, Conditions.
CSH-100.x:
Basis: Trade credit practice (the 5Cs).
Analysis: The 5Cs are Character (reputation, payment record), Capacity (ability to repay), Capital (equity, financial strength), Collateral (security), Conditions (economy, industry).
Distractors: A – Currency isn't one of the 5Cs (currency risk is a separate factor).

CSH-101.q: Match each C with what it assesses:
CSH-101.e: Capital (equity, financial strength) is the fifth C.
p: Ability to repay from operating cash flow
Economic and industry environment of the customer
CSH-101.x:
Basis: The 5Cs model.
Analysis: Character – willingness and payment history (credit bureau checks, trading experience); Capacity – repayment from operating cash flow; Collateral – security, guarantees; Conditions – the customer's economic and industry context. Capital (equity, leverage) is the fifth.

CSH-102.q: Arrange the debt collection escalation sequence:
CSH-102.e: Escalating from soft to hard actions preserves relationships while controlling risk.
o: Call/email as soon as the invoice is overdue
Formal notice and suspension of deliveries
CSH-102.x:
Basis: Trade credit practice; Circular 48/2019/TT-BTC.
Analysis: Escalation from soft to hard: pre-due reminder → call/email at due date → formal notice and credit hold → demand letter, legal referral or lawsuit → provisioning and write-off per regulations (with full documentation – ACC-051). It preserves good customer relationships without letting debts linger.

CSH-103.q: Under Circular 48/2019/TT-BTC, receivables overdue from 6 months to under 1 year are provided at 30%.
CSH-103.e: True. Rates: 30% (6 months–<1 year), 50% (1–<2 years), 70% (2–<3 years), 100% (3 years or more).
CSH-103.x:
Basis: Circular 48/2019/TT-BTC.
Analysis: True. Maximum rates: 6 months to under 1 year overdue – 30%; 1 to under 2 years – 50%; 2 to under 3 years – 70%; 3 years or more – 100% (ACC-050).

CSH-104.q: A receivable of VND 200 million is 14 months overdue. Under Circular 48/2019/TT-BTC, what provision is required?
CSH-104.x:
Basis: Circular 48/2019/TT-BTC.
Working: 14 months overdue falls in 1 to under 2 years → 50% × 200 = 100 million VND (ACC-051).

CSH-105.q: Consider these statements on provision rates for overdue receivables under Circular 48/2019/TT-BTC:
CSH-105.e: The correct rate for 2–<3 years overdue is 70%.
CSH-105.x:
Basis: Circular 48/2019/TT-BTC.
Analysis: True: 6 months to under 1 year – 30%; 1 to under 2 years – 50%; 3 years or more – 100%. False: 2 to under 3 years is 70%, not 80%.

CSH-106.q: Inventory turnover of 9.125 times per year corresponds to average days in inventory of about:
CSH-106.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice.
Working: Days in inventory = 365 / 9.125 = 40 days.
Distractors: 9, 91 and 36 days are miscalculated.

CSH-107.q: Annual demand D = 10,000 units; ordering cost VND 800,000 per order; holding cost VND 4,000 per unit per year. EOQ = 2,000 units. How many orders are placed per year?

CSH-108.q: Annual demand D = 10,000 units; ordering cost S = VND 800,000 per order; holding cost H = VND 4,000 per unit per year; EOQ = 2,000 units. What is total annual ordering plus holding cost at EOQ (VND)?
CSH-108.x:
Basis: EOQ model.
Working: Ordering = D/Q × S = 5 × 800,000 = 4,000,000; holding = Q/2 × H = 1,000 × 4,000 = 4,000,000. Total = 8,000,000 VND.
Note: The two are equal at EOQ (CSH-109); total = √(2DSH) = √(2 × 10,000 × 800,000 × 4,000) = 8,000,000.

CSH-109.q: At EOQ, annual ordering cost equals annual holding cost.
CSH-109.e: True. This characterises the optimum in the basic EOQ model.
CSH-109.x:
Basis: Basic EOQ model.
Analysis: True. Total cost TC(Q) = DS/Q + QH/2; its derivative is zero when DS/Q² = H/2 ⇔ DS/Q = QH/2 – ordering cost equals holding cost at the optimum (e.g., CSH-108: 4 million = 4 million).

CSH-110.q: The biggest risk of Just-in-Time (JIT) inventory is:
CSH-110.e: JIT minimises inventory and therefore depends on supply chain reliability.
o: Production disruption when suppliers deliver late
CSH-110.x:
Basis: Supply chain practice (Toyota Production System).
Analysis: JIT minimises stock, receiving goods just when needed → it depends entirely on supplier and logistics reliability; late deliveries stop the line. The pandemic and the 2020–2022 chip shortage exposed this risk.
Distractors: B and C are JIT strengths (less holding, obsolescence); D is unrelated.

CSH-111.q: Maximum usage 70 units/day, average 50; maximum lead time 10 days, average 8. Safety stock (= max usage × max lead time − average usage × average lead time) is how many units?
CSH-111.x:
Basis: Inventory management practice.
Working: Safety stock = 70 × 10 − 50 × 8 = 700 − 400 = 300 units.
Note: This is the simple max-minus-average method; the statistical method uses z × σ for a target service level. Reorder point = 50 × 8 + 300 = 700 units.

CSH-112.q: Select ALL signs of slow-moving/obsolete inventory warranting provision review:
CSH-112.e: Fast-selling, newly received items are not a sign of obsolescence.
o: Items whose turnover dropped sharply versus the prior period
Quantities exceeding 12 months of expected sales
CSH-112.x:
Basis: VAS 02; Circular 48/2019/TT-BTC (inventory write-downs).
Analysis: Signs needing an allowance review: (A) sharply falling turnover – weakening demand; (B) near expiry – lower NRV; (C) stock above 12 months' expected sales – risk of not selling at cost.
Distractors: (D) Fast-selling new stock has high NRV, not a sign of obsolescence.

CSH-113.q: Holding costs include cost of capital, storage, insurance, shrinkage and obsolescence risk.
CSH-113.e: True. Cost of capital is often the largest component but frequently overlooked.
CSH-113.x:
Basis: Inventory management practice.
Analysis: True. Holding cost (H) covers: capital tied up (interest or opportunity cost), storage, warehouse operations, insurance, shrinkage, theft, obsolescence and expiry. Capital cost is often the largest (commonly 8–15% of stock value a year) but overlooked because no invoice shows it – leading to overstocking.

CSH-114.q: Under '1/10, net 40', the opportunity cost (simple annual rate, 365 days) of NOT taking the discount is about:
CSH-114.e: 1/99 × 365/30 ≈ 12.3% per year. If bank rates are lower, borrow to take the discount.
CSH-114.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Working: 1 / (100 − 1) × 365 / (40 − 10) = 0.010101 × 12.167 ≈ 12.3% a year.
Note: With bank interest at 9% < 12.3% → borrow and take the discount; if borrowing costs exceed 12.3%, use the full 40 days.

CSH-115.q: Terms are '3/15, net 45'. What is the simple annual opportunity cost (365 days) of forgoing the discount (%, 1 decimal)?
CSH-115.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Working: 3 / 97 × 365 / (45 − 15) = 0.030928 × 12.1667 ≈ 0.3763 → 37.6% a year.

CSH-116.q: Under '2/10, net 30', having decided not to take the discount, the business should pay on day 30 rather than earlier.
CSH-116.e: True. Once the discount is forgone, use the full free credit period – but do not pay late.
CSH-116.x:
Basis: Working capital practice.
Analysis: True. Once the discount is forgone, paying before day 30 gains nothing – use the remaining free credit to keep the cash. But don't pay after day 30, which damages credibility and may incur penalties (CSH-048).

CSH-117.q: A VND 1 billion, 1-year loan at a nominal 10% with interest deducted upfront (discount loan). The effective rate is about:
CSH-117.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice (discount loans – interest in advance).
Working: Interest = 1,000 × 10% = 100 million, deducted at drawdown → 900 million received. Effective rate = 100 / 900 = 11.11%.
Distractors: 10% is nominal; 9.09% is inverted (100/1,100); 12% has no basis.

CSH-118.q: A credit line of VND 20 billion has average usage of 12 billion; the commitment fee is 0.5% per year on the unused portion. What is the annual commitment fee?
CSH-118.x:
Basis: Bank lending practice.
Working: Undrawn = 20 − 12 = 8 billion. Commitment fee = 8 billion × 0.5% = 40 million VND a year.
Note: The line's true cost = interest on drawn amounts + commitment fees; oversizing it raises costs.

CSH-119.q: Continuously rolling short-term loans to finance long-term assets creates refinancing risk when banks tighten credit.
CSH-119.e: True. This is maturity mismatch risk.
CSH-119.x:
Basis: Matching principle (CSH-051, CSH-052).
Analysis: True. Funding long-term assets by continually rolling short-term debt creates maturity mismatch: when banks tighten (credit growth caps, rate rises), the firm can't roll over while assets haven't generated enough cash – forcing fire sales or insolvency.

CSH-120.e: The aggressive strategy maximises short-term debt; the conservative one relies more on long-term sources.
o: Uses short-term debt to fund part of permanent current assets – lower cost, higher risk
Uses long-term sources for all assets
CSH-120.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice (working capital financing strategies).
Analysis: The aggressive strategy uses short-term debt for fluctuating current assets and part of permanent current assets – cheaper (short rates are usually lower) but with more refinancing and rate risk.
Distractors: B and C are conservative; D is liquidity caution, not an aggressive financing strategy.

CSH-121.q: Match each working capital financing strategy with its feature:
CSH-121.e: The three strategies trade off cost of capital against liquidity risk.
p: Long-term funds finance permanent assets and part of fluctuating assets
Short-term debt funds part of permanent assets
CSH-121.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice.
Analysis: Conservative – long-term funds cover permanent assets and some fluctuating ones (safe, costly, sometimes surplus cash); matching – funding maturity mirrors asset life; aggressive – short-term debt covers part of permanent assets (cheap, risky). The three trade capital cost against liquidity risk.

CSH-122.q: Select ALL early-warning signals of a liquidity crisis:
CSH-122.e: Stable DSO and on-time customer payments are positive signs.
o: Negative operating cash flow for several consecutive quarters
Growing reliance on rolling short-term debt
Late payment of taxes and social insurance
Stable DSO with customers paying on time
CSH-122.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice; VSA 570 (going-concern indicators).
Analysis: Warning signs: (A) negative OCF for several quarters; (B) growing reliance on rolling short-term debt; (C) late tax and social insurance payments – usually the first things 'sacrificed'; (D) suppliers demanding prepayment – the market has lost credit confidence.
Distractors: (E) Stable DSO with customers paying on time is positive.

CSH-123.e: True. The lower the ratio, the higher the risk of failing to pay interest.
CSH-123.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice.
Analysis: True. Interest cover = EBIT / interest expense – how many times operating profit covers interest. The lower (e.g., < 1.5), the higher the risk of missing interest; banks often set minimum covenants. An EBITDA version suits depreciation-heavy firms.

CSH-124.q: EBIT is VND 30 billion; interest expense 6 billion. What is interest coverage?
CSH-124.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice (interest coverage – times interest earned).
Working: Interest cover = EBIT / interest expense = 30 / 6 = 5×.
Analysis: EBIT is 5× interest → EBIT could fall 80% before failing to cover interest – a decent buffer. Banks often require covenants ≥ 2–3×; below 1.5× is a risk zone. Also use EBITDA/interest and DSCR (including principal due), since principal repayments are the bigger cash strain.

CSH-125.q: Total borrowings VND 80 billion, cash and equivalents 20 billion, EBITDA 30 billion. What is Net debt/EBITDA?
CSH-125.x:
Basis: Bank lending practice.
Working: Net debt = 80 − 20 = 60 billion. Net debt/EBITDA = 60 / 30 = 2 times – about 2 years of EBITDA to repay net debt.
Note: Banks typically cap it at 3–4x depending on industry; under IFRS 16 lease liabilities raise both net debt and EBITDA (IFR-074).

CSH-126.q: An importer must pay USD 1 million in 3 months and buys USD forward at 26,500 VND/USD. What VND cost is locked in?
CSH-126.e: 1,000,000 × 26,500 = VND 26.5 billion, regardless of the spot rate at maturity.
CSH-126.x:
Basis: FX risk management practice.
Working: Locked VND cost = 1,000,000 × 26,500 = 26,500,000,000 VND = 26.5 billion VND, whatever the spot rate at maturity.

CSH-127.q: An FX forward eliminates both downside risk and the upside if rates move favourably.
CSH-127.e: True. To keep the upside, use an option, which requires a premium.
CSH-127.x:
Basis: FX risk management practice.
Analysis: True. A forward is a two-way obligation: you must buy at the locked rate – protected if USD rises, but missing out if it falls (e.g., CSH-126: if USD drops to 26,000 you still pay 26.5 billion instead of 26). To keep the upside, use an option and pay a premium (CSH-128).

CSH-128.q: Feature of an FX call option for an importer:
CSH-128.e: An option protects against rate rises while keeping the benefit if rates fall.
o: A right but not an obligation to buy currency at the strike rate; premium paid upfront
An obligation to buy at a fixed rate with no fee
Selling currency to the bank at spot
CSH-128.x:
Basis: FX risk management practice.
Analysis: A currency call option gives the holder the right but not the obligation to buy at the strike, for an upfront premium. If the rate rises above the strike → exercise (protected); if it falls → lapse and buy spot more cheaply (losing only the premium).
Distractors: B is a forward; C is an interest rate swap; D is a spot deal.

CSH-129.q: Arrange the steps to build and run a 13-week cash forecast:
CSH-129.e: The 13-week forecast is a rolling tool updated weekly.
o: Forecast receipts by customer and due date
Forecast scheduled payments (payroll, suppliers, tax, debt)
Compute weekly net cash flow and closing balance vs. minimum
Compare actual with forecast weekly and roll forward one week
CSH-129.x:
Basis: Treasury management practice.
Analysis: Order: (1) bank-reconciled opening balance – an accurate start; (2) receipts by customer and due date (adjusted for late-payment habits); (3) payments by schedule (payroll, suppliers, tax, debt); (4) weekly net flow and closing balance against the minimum; (5) weekly actual-versus-forecast review, rolling one week forward (CSH-024).

CSH-130.q: Consider these statements on the indirect cash flow statement (form B03-DN):
CSH-130.e: An inventory increase reduces cash flow and must be deducted.
o: It starts from profit before tax.
An increase in inventory is added to profit.
Proceeds from share issuance are financing activities.
CSH-130.x:
Basis: VAS 24; form B03-DN (Circular 99/2025/TT-BTC).
Analysis: True: the VAS 24 indirect method starts from profit before tax; depreciation is added back (non-cash); share-issue proceeds are financing. False: rising inventory consumes cash, so it's deducted, not added (CSH-075).

CSH-131.q: A company growing revenue 40% is profitable but short of cash for payroll. The most sensible priority is:
CSH-131.e: Growth-driven cash shortage (overtrading) requires working capital action and matching finance; late SI triggers penalties and legal risk.
o: Review receivables and inventory to release cash, and arrange short-term credit lines matching the growth
Cut prices sharply to boost revenue
CSH-131.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice; Social Insurance Law 41/2024/QH15 (late contributions).
Analysis: Cash shortage from overtrading (CSH-012) needs root fixes: review receivables (collections, tighter credit) and stock (clear slow movers) to free cash, and arrange short-term lines sized to the new working capital (CSH-132).
Distractors: B cuts margins and may add working capital; C misuses funds, draining cash; D – late social insurance incurs interest, penalties and legal risk.

CSH-132.q: Net working capital requirement is 20% of revenue. Revenue is expected to grow from VND 500 to 650 billion. What is the additional working capital need?
CSH-132.x:
Basis: Corporate finance practice (percentage-of-sales method).
Working: Extra working capital = (650 − 500) × 20% = 150 × 20% = 30 billion VND.
Note: Compare with expected retained earnings to size external funding.

CSH-133.q: Holding excessive idle cash has an opportunity cost equal to the return forgone from investing or repaying debt.
CSH-133.e: True. The minimum cash level should rest on cash forecasts and standby credit lines.
CSH-133.x:
Basis: Treasury practice.
Analysis: True. Idle cash beyond needs carries an opportunity cost: forgone yield (deposits, short-term investments) or interest that paying down debt would save – borrowing rates usually exceed deposit rates, so holding cash while borrowing is costly. Cash levels should rest on forecasts and standby lines (CSH-072, CSH-057).

CSH-134.q: A Zero Balance Account (ZBA) is used to:
CSH-134.e: ZBA is a cash concentration tool that reduces idle cash scattered across accounts.
o: Automatically sweep sub-account balances to a master account at day-end, centralising liquidity
CSH-134.x:
Basis: Treasury practice (cash concentration).
Analysis: In a ZBA structure, sub-accounts (branches, collections, disbursements) are swept to the master account daily (and funded when payments are due), leaving zero balances – concentrating liquidity, cutting scattered idle cash and borrowing.
Distractors: B misreads the name; C – reconciliation is still needed; D is unrelated to tax.

CSH-135.q: When analysing cash flow, one-off receipts (asset sales, compensation) should be excluded to assess sustainable cash generation from core operations.
CSH-135.e: True. Normalised cash flow reflects recurring cash-generating capacity.
CSH-135.x:
Basis: Financial analysis practice (normalised cash flow).
Analysis: True. One-off receipts (asset sales, insurance settlements, one-time tax refunds) don't recur; keeping them overstates cash-generating ability. Normalised cash flow strips them and one-time working capital swings – reflecting sustainable cash generation for valuation and credit appraisal.
